h1: Designing a lager for drinkers in hot countries
title: Designing a Lager for Hot Countries | Craft Beer School
desc: How to build a lager that tastes clean and refreshing at 35 °C ambient: gravity, bitterness, adjuncts, carbonation, yeast and serving.
teaser: A lager for a hot afternoon is judged cold, fast and in large gulps. Design for that drinker, not for the competition table.
standfirst: Light colour, modest bitterness, high attenuation and brisk carbonation make a lager that still tastes good as it warms in the glass. Here is the recipe logic and the process behind it.
sections:
The person drinking your lager is hot, thirsty and probably eating spicy or salty food. They want a cold beer they can finish before it warms and that does not feel heavy. That points to a pale, dry, clean lager of moderate strength. It does not rule out character, but any flavour has to survive being cold and then being not so cold.

Flavours that read as pleasant at 12 °C can turn sticky or cloying at 25 °C. Residual sweetness, diacetyl and fruity esters all become louder as beer warms. A hot-country lager must be clean enough to tolerate that.

Most beers aimed at hot-weather drinking sit between 4.0 and 5.0 per cent ABV, from an original gravity of about 1.040 to 1.048 and a final gravity of about 1.006 to 1.010. Use ABV = (OG - FG) x 131.25 to check: 1.044 to 1.008 gives 4.7 per cent. A high degree of attenuation, with fermentation going close to the limit, gives a dry finish that suits heat.

Mash for fermentability. A saccharification rest around 63 to 65 °C (145 to 149 °F) produces more fermentable sugar than a rest at 68 to 70 °C. Hold it long enough for conversion to finish. Test with iodine if you are unsure.

A grist of mostly pilsner malt gives a pale, clean base. Many brewers use some rice or maize (corn) to lighten body and flavour. Both are almost pure starch with little protein, so they ferment out dry and add little colour. Typical use is 10 to 30 per cent of the grist, with specific details in our guide to cooking rice in the brewhouse. Aim for about 6 to 8 EBC. Avoid crystal malts, which leave sweetness behind.

If you are curious about the broader tradition, read about Asian rice lagers.

Bitterness of about 10 to 20 IBU is common in this style. That is enough to balance the malt without leaving a lingering edge. Choose noble-type or other clean hops and add most of them early. Avoid heavy late additions, because hop aroma fades quickly in warm storage, as our guide on the hot-country cold chain explains. You can use a little aroma hop for lift. Just do not rely on it surviving.

Watch the water. Soft, low-mineral water suits pale lagers. Aim for calcium around 50 mg/L, low sulphate and a mash pH of 5.2 to 5.6.

The classic lager route is bottom-fermenting yeast at 8 to 13 °C (46 to 55 °F), followed by a diacetyl rest a few degrees warmer and then cold conditioning. If you cannot hold those temperatures, you have options. Some lager strains tolerate warmer fermentation, around 15 to 20 °C, though with more esters. Some breweries use clean ale strains at the cool end of their range to make a lager-like beer. Be honest on the label: a warm-fermented clean beer is not a traditional lager, even if it drinks like one.

Pitch plenty of healthy yeast. Lager yeast needs about twice the cells of an ale per degree Plato. Under-pitching is a common cause of diacetyl and sulphur problems. Heat makes it worse.

Hot-weather drinkers like a lively beer. Carbonation around 2.5 to 2.8 volumes of CO2 gives the prickle that feels refreshing. Serve at 2 to 4 °C (36 to 39 °F) for a lager of this kind. Cans protect against light and oxygen and cool quickly, which suits the market.

Think about glass size too. A small glass kept cold beats a large pint that warms before the end. That is a commercial point as much as a brewing one. It affects how your beer is judged.
Test it where it will be drunk

Taste the beer warm. Pour a sample, leave it for 20 minutes in the heat, then taste it again. If it gets worse fast, find the cause: sweetness, esters, bitterness or oxygen damage. Fix the recipe, not the drinker. Do the same with a sample aged for two weeks at your market temperature. If you want to go deeper into style design, the broader picture is in our map of world beer styles.
faqs: What ABV suits a hot-weather lager?
Between 4 and 5 per cent is common. The beer should be easy to finish and not heavy.
Can I make a lager without cold fermentation?
You can make a clean beer using warm-tolerant lager yeast or a clean ale yeast at its cool end. It will differ from a classic lager, so be honest about it.
Why use rice or maize in a lager?
Both lighten body and colour and help the beer finish dry. They are almost all starch with little protein or flavour of their own.
How cold should I serve it?
About 2 to 4 °C is typical for a light lager. Colder numbs the flavour. Warmer exposes any sweetness or off-flavour.
